title: Infectious Urinary Diseases: Pyelonephritis, Cystitis, and Urethritis
subject: Renal and Urinary System (RENL)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows infection up and down the urinary tract: urethritis at the outlet, cystitis in the bladder, and acute pyelonephritis in the kidney. Each level has its own defenses, risk factors, symptoms, and urine findings, and board questions nearly always ask you to place the infection at the correct level from those clues, name the likely organism, and predict what happens if it spreads. The organisms themselves are covered in UR-11; here the focus is on how host anatomy and the inflammatory response explain the presentation, the laboratory findings, and the complications.
prerequisites: Gross anatomy of the kidney, ureter, bladder, and urethra in both sexes (UR-3, UR-4)
Nephron histology, urothelium, and the renal papillae (UR-2)
Micturition reflex and its afferent and efferent pathways (UR-6)
Urinary pathogens, virulence factors, and urinalysis in infection (UR-11)
Acute inflammation: neutrophil recruitment, cytokines, and fever

connections.how: Fimbriae, urease, pili, and intracellular life cycles explain which organism causes which level of infection and why some escape the Gram stain.
Obstruction causes urinary stasis that favors infection, and urease-producing infection forms struvite stones that worsen obstruction.

connections.to: Inflammatory and congenital urinary disease (UR-12-D, UR-12-E)
connections.how: Vesicoureteral reflux and repeated acute pyelonephritis lead to chronic pyelonephritis, and papillary necrosis is shared with analgesic nephropathy.
Gonococcal and chlamydial urethritis ascend along continuous mucosa to cause epididymitis in men and pelvic inflammatory disease in women.
Reactive arthritis after Chlamydia and disseminated gonococcal infection with terminal complement deficiency link urethral infection to the joints.

terms.def: Suppurative bacterial infection of the renal pelvis and tubulointerstitium, usually reached by ascent from the bladder.
Inflammation of the bladder mucosa, in this chapter caused by bacterial infection confined to the lower tract.
Inflammation of the urethra, usually from a sexually transmitted infection, classified as gonococcal or nongonococcal.
Neutrophils in the urine, detected as leukocyte esterase on dipstick or as white cells on microscopy.
Pyuria with a negative routine urine culture, which points to organisms that do not grow on standard media or to noninfectious inflammation.
A cylinder of uromodulin matrix packed with leukocytes that forms in a tubule lumen and proves the leukocytes came from the kidney.
The angle between the 12th rib and the lateral border of the erector spinae muscles, overlying the kidney, where percussion tenderness suggests renal inflammation.
Ischemic death of the renal papillary tips, which may slough into the collecting system.
Pus filling an obstructed renal pelvis and calyces, which cannot drain.
A collection of pus that has broken through the renal capsule into the perinephric fat.
Ascending infection of the upper female genital tract (endometrium, fallopian tubes, ovaries, pelvic peritoneum), usually from cervical gonococcal or chlamydial infection.
A sterile inflammatory arthritis that follows a genitourinary or enteric infection, often with urethritis and conjunctivitis, and is associated with HLA-B27.

blocks.text: Acute pyelonephritis is suppurative (pus-forming) bacterial infection of the renal pelvis and tubulointerstitium. Most cases are ascending: enteric gram-negative rods, above all uropathogenic Escherichia coli, colonize the periurethral area, enter the bladder, and then climb the ureter. The kidney is normally protected because ureteral peristalsis carries urine downward and the oblique course of the ureter through the bladder wall closes during voiding, acting as a one-way valve. Vesicoureteral reflux, obstruction, and the ureteral dilation of pregnancy defeat this valve, and P fimbriae, which bind glycolipid receptors on upper tract urothelium (UR-11), let bacteria hold on against urine flow.

Infected urine in the pelvis can be forced into the collecting ducts through the flattened compound papillae at the renal poles (intrarenal reflux), so ascending infection and its later scars favor the poles. Less often, infection is hematogenous, classically Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia seeding the cortex with multiple small abscesses.

blocks.title: The ascending route to the kidney
steps: Fecal flora colonize the periurethral area
Bacteria ascend the urethra into the bladder
Type 1 fimbriae attach bacteria to bladder urothelium
Reflux or obstruction carries infected urine up the ureter
P fimbriae anchor bacteria in the renal pelvis
Intrarenal reflux delivers bacteria into collecting ducts
Neutrophils fill the interstitium and tubules
blocks.caption: Each step must overcome a host defense; reflux and obstruction are the usual reasons the kidney is reached.

blocks.text: Grossly, the kidney is swollen, with discrete yellow-white abscesses raised on the cortical surface. Microscopically the hallmark is patchy suppurative inflammation of the interstitium, with neutrophils packing the tubular lumens and destroying tubules in the most intense foci. Glomeruli are relatively resistant to infection and are spared early. This tubulointerstitial pattern is the key contrast with glomerulonephritis, which produces red cell casts and proteinuria instead.

The symptoms follow from the inflammation. Cytokines from the infected parenchyma (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha) induce prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus, raising the temperature set point and causing fever, usually above 38 °C (100.4 °F), with chills. Edema stretches the renal capsule, producing dull flank pain and tenderness when the costovertebral angle is percussed, often with nausea and vomiting. Because the infection usually passes through the bladder, dysuria and frequency often come first. The blood shows a neutrophilic leukocytosis, and the urine shows pyuria, bacteriuria, and WBC casts. Casts form only inside tubules, where uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein) secreted by the thick ascending limb gels around trapped cells, so a WBC cast places the leukocytes in the kidney. WBC casts are not specific for infection, because acute interstitial nephritis also produces them (UR-12-D).

blocks.title: Complications of acute pyelonephritis
rows: Papillary tips lie at the end of the medullary blood supply; inflammatory edema and microvascular disease cut off flow and infarct them
Diabetes, obstruction, or sickle cell disease; sloughed papillae cause colic, hematuria, or obstruction
Suppurative foci coalesce, or blood-borne S. aureus seeds the cortex
Persistent fever and a focal mass on imaging
High-grade obstruction, often a stone, traps pus in the pelvis and calyces
Dilated, pus-filled collecting system; high sepsis risk
Suppuration breaks through the capsule into perinephric fat
Fever outlasting the expected course, flank mass
Lipid A of lipopolysaccharide activates TLR4, releasing cytokines that cause vasodilation and capillary leak
Hypotension and organ failure, especially with obstruction
blocks.caption: Obstruction and diabetes underlie most severe complications; repeated infection with reflux or obstruction leads to chronic pyelonephritis (UR-12-D).

blocks.predict: A patient with long-standing diabetes is being followed for acute pyelonephritis and suddenly develops colicky flank pain, gross hematuria, and fragments of tissue in the urine. What has happened?
blocks.explain: Papillary necrosis. The papillae are poorly perfused tips of the medulla, and diabetic microvascular disease plus inflammatory edema infarcts them; a sloughed papilla passing down the ureter causes colic, bleeding, and possible obstruction.
blocks.check: Compare with the complications table and the description of papillary blood supply.

sections.title: Cystitis: risk factors and how it differs from pyelonephritis

blocks.text: The bladder stays sterile mainly because voiding flushes it often and almost completely. In addition, a glycosaminoglycan layer and uroplakin plaques cover the urothelium, uromodulin in the urine binds type 1 fimbriae as a soluble decoy, infected superficial (umbrella) cells are shed, and vaginal lactobacilli keep the introital pH low enough to limit colonization by enteric bacteria. Each risk factor for cystitis defeats one of these defenses.

blocks.title: Risk factors for cystitis and the defense each one defeats
rows: Short urethra (about 4 cm versus about 20 cm in men) opening near the vagina and anus
Pushes periurethral bacteria into the bladder; spermicides disturb vaginal flora
Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle and the uterus compresses the ureters, causing stasis and easy ascent
Bypass the urethra and carry a biofilm shielded from urine flow; risk rises each day
Glycosuria, impaired neutrophil function, and neuropathic incomplete emptying
Prostatic enlargement, stones, strictures, or neurogenic bladder leave residual urine
Loss of estrogen and vaginal lactobacilli allows enteric colonization
blocks.caption: The long male urethra and antibacterial prostatic secretions make cystitis in men uncommon, so it suggests obstruction or instrumentation.

blocks.title: Obstruction and infection reinforce each other
steps: Urease organisms such as Proteus alkalinize urine
Struvite precipitates and forms a stone
The stone worsens obstruction and shelters bacteria
blocks.caption: Stones and infection sustain each other (UR-12-C).

blocks.text: Cystitis causes dysuria (burning as urine passes over the inflamed trigone and urethra), frequency, and urgency, because inflammation sensitizes bladder stretch afferents so that the micturition reflex fires at small volumes. Suprapubic pain and tenderness are common, and the hyperemic mucosa may bleed enough to cause gross hematuria. The infection is confined to the superficial mucosa, so little cytokine reaches the circulation: there is no fever, no flank pain, and no casts. Elderly patients may present only with confusion or new incontinence.

Urinalysis shows pyuria (positive leukocyte esterase), bacteriuria, and often a positive nitrite test, which requires an organism with nitrate reductase and several hours of urine dwell time (UR-11). Enterococcus and Staphylococcus saprophyticus usually do not form nitrite, and the frequent voiding of cystitis shortens dwell time, so a negative nitrite does not exclude infection.

blocks.title: Placing the infection at the correct level
rows: E. coli, S. saprophyticus, Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterococcus
E. coli and other enteric gram-negative rods
blocks.caption: Fever, flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, and WBC casts mark the kidney; discharge and a negative routine culture mark the urethra.

blocks.title: Worked example: localizing a urinary infection
blocks.text: A 24-year-old woman has 3 days of dysuria and frequency. Today she has a temperature of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), chills, and right costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis shows positive leukocyte esterase, negative nitrite, bacteria, and WBC casts. Step 1: dysuria and frequency place infection in the bladder. Step 2: fever, flank tenderness, and WBC casts mean the renal parenchyma is now involved, so this is acute pyelonephritis that began as cystitis. Step 3: the negative nitrite does not argue against infection, for the reasons above. Step 4: there is no discharge and bacteriuria is present, so urethritis is not the explanation.

blocks.predict: Why does an indwelling catheter raise infection risk even though it keeps the bladder empty?
blocks.explain: Complete emptying is only one defense. The catheter bypasses the urethra, gives bacteria a path along its surfaces, and supports a biofilm protected from urine flow and neutrophils.
blocks.check: Compare with the defenses paragraph and the risk factor table.

sections.title: Gonococcal and nongonococcal urethritis and their complications

blocks.text: Urethritis presents with dysuria and urethral discharge and is usually sexually transmitted. It is divided by Gram stain into gonococcal urethritis (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) and nongonococcal urethritis, most often from Chlamydia trachomatis serovars D to K. Their biology (UR-11) explains why the two forms look different.

Gonococci attach to nonciliated columnar epithelium by pili and Opa proteins, cross it by transcytosis, and release lipooligosaccharide that triggers an intense neutrophil response. The result is a heavy, purulent discharge, and Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils, a finding highly sensitive in symptomatic men. Women are more often asymptomatic or present with cervicitis. Chlamydia is obligate intracellular: the infectious elementary body enters the cell and becomes a replicating reticulate body inside an inclusion. Few organisms are free in the discharge and inflammation is milder, so discharge is scant or absent and many infections are silent. Gram stain shows neutrophils without organisms and routine culture is negative (sterile pyuria). Nucleic acid amplification testing detects both, and coinfection is common.

blocks.title: Gonococcal versus nongonococcal urethritis
rows: C. trachomatis serovars D to K; also M. genitalium, Ureaplasma, T. vaginalis
Scant, watery or mucoid, or none
Common in women, less so in men
blocks.caption: Both organisms cause epididymitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and neonatal conjunctivitis.

blocks.text: Untreated infection spreads along continuous mucosa. In men it travels through the ejaculatory duct and ductus deferens to the epididymis, causing unilateral scrotal pain and swelling; epididymitis is usually chlamydial or gonococcal in younger men but caused by enteric rods with obstruction or instrumentation in older men. Gonococcal urethritis can also heal with fibrosis and urethral stricture. In women, infection ascends from the cervix through the endometrium to the fallopian tubes. Tubal scarring means even silent chlamydial infection can cause infertility and ectopic pregnancy.

blocks.title: Ascending infection in women
steps: Healing with tubal scarring and adhesions
Infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain
blocks.caption: Pelvic inflammatory disease; tubal spread to the liver capsule causes perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome).

blocks.text: Two complications reach beyond the genital tract. Reactive arthritis follows chlamydial urethritis (or enteric infection) by a few weeks, most often in HLA-B27 positive people. It is an immune reaction to bacterial antigens, not joint infection, so synovial fluid culture is negative; it causes asymmetric lower limb arthritis, enthesitis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis. Disseminated gonococcal infection follows bacteremia, causing tenosynovitis, polyarthralgia, and sparse pustular skin lesions, or a purulent monoarthritis, often of the knee. Because the membrane attack complex is needed to kill Neisseria, deficiency of terminal complement components (C5 to C9) predisposes to recurrent neisserial infection.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading urethritis findings
blocks.text: A 22-year-old man has mild dysuria and a scant mucoid discharge 10 days after a new sexual partner. Gram stain shows neutrophils but no organisms, and routine urine culture is negative. Step 1: discharge with pyuria means urethritis. Step 2: no intracellular diplococci, scant discharge, and onset after more than a week favor nongonococcal urethritis, most likely Chlamydia, which does not grow on routine media. Step 3: three weeks later he develops a swollen knee, heel pain, and red eyes. This is reactive arthritis, and joint fluid culture would be sterile because the arthritis is immune mediated.

blocks.predict: Why can a woman with no symptoms of chlamydial infection still become infertile?
blocks.explain: Chlamydia causes little acute inflammation, so it can ascend to the tubes silently, yet the low-grade inflammation still heals with scarring that blocks or distorts them.
blocks.check: Compare with the ascending infection flow and the description of the chlamydial life cycle.

integration.text: Anatomy sets the risk at every level: a short female urethra near the perineum explains why cystitis is common in women, the vesicoureteral valve explains why most bladder infections stay in the bladder, and compound polar papillae explain where ascending infection and later scars concentrate. Microbiology explains the organism and the stain: adhesive fimbriae for E. coli, urease for Proteus, pili and lipooligosaccharide for gonococci, and an intracellular cycle for Chlamydia that hides it from the Gram stain and routine culture. Immunology and pathology explain the findings: neutrophils produce pyuria, leukocyte esterase, and WBC casts; cytokines produce fever; lipopolysaccharide produces septic shock; and HLA-B27 and terminal complement deficiency explain reactive arthritis and recurrent neisserial infection.

These distinctions have limits. Fever and flank pain can be blunted in the elderly, in diabetes, and in immunosuppression, WBC casts are often missed on microscopy and also occur in interstitial nephritis, and a negative nitrite or a modest colony count does not exclude infection. Sterile pyuria has a differential beyond urethritis, including renal tuberculosis and interstitial nephritis (UR-11, UR-12-D), so each finding is read with the whole clinical picture.

summary: Most urinary infections ascend from periurethral fecal flora; E. coli with type 1 fimbriae colonizes the bladder and P fimbriae help it reach the kidney.
Vesicoureteral reflux, obstruction, and the ureteral dilation of pregnancy let bladder infection reach the kidney; hematogenous S. aureus infection is less common.

Acute pyelonephritis is patchy neutrophilic inflammation of the interstitium and tubules with glomeruli spared; fever, flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, and WBC casts place it in the kidney.
Complications of pyelonephritis are papillary necrosis, renal and perinephric abscess, pyonephrosis behind an obstruction, and urosepsis from lipopolysaccharide.
Risk factors for cystitis each defeat a defense: short female urethra, intercourse, pregnancy, catheters, diabetes, obstruction, and estrogen loss.
Cystitis causes dysuria, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic pain without fever, flank pain, or casts because infection stays in the superficial mucosa.
A negative nitrite does not exclude infection: Enterococcus and S. saprophyticus lack nitrate reductase, and frequent voiding shortens dwell time.
Gonococcal urethritis gives a purulent discharge with intracellular gram-negative diplococci; chlamydial urethritis gives scant discharge, no organisms on Gram stain, and sterile pyuria.
Urethral infection ascends to cause epididymitis in men and pelvic inflammatory disease with tubal scarring, infertility, and perihepatitis in women.
Chlamydia can trigger sterile reactive arthritis in HLA-B27 positive people; gonococcal bacteremia causes disseminated infection, favored by terminal complement deficiency.

verify: Urine culture thresholds for significant bacteriuria (classically 100,000 CFU/mL, with lower counts accepted in symptomatic patients and catheter specimens) vary among sources; confirm the values NABNE expects before adding them.
Incubation periods (gonococcal usually 2 to 7 days, chlamydial usually 1 to 3 weeks) are stated as approximate and differ slightly among references.
The age cutoff separating sexually transmitted from enteric epididymitis (often given as 35 years) comes from clinical guidance and varies; this chapter states it descriptively.
Urethral length (about 4 cm in women and about 20 cm in men) varies by source; ranges of 3 to 5 cm and 18 to 22 cm are quoted.
The proportion of untreated bacteriuria in pregnancy that progresses to pyelonephritis is quoted variously (often 20 to 40 percent); the chapter gives no figure.

Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome and Tamm-Horsfall protein or only the descriptive terms (perihepatitis, uromodulin), and whether the older eponym for reactive arthritis is avoided.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: uti-levels (urethra, bladder, ureter, and kidney with the findings at each level) and pyelo-histology (neutrophils in tubules and interstitium with a WBC cast).
